theme: Bless the LORD, O my soul, steadfast love as high as heaven
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 103. After a psalm of exhaustion, here is a psalm of praise, one of the most loved in the whole Psalter. You may have read it before. Read it slowly, and let every phrase about forgiveness sink in.
settingTheScene: Psalm 103 is a psalm of David. It is an individual’s call to himself to bless the LORD, which widens out to include all God’s people and all creation. After Jeremiah’s relentless warnings and Psalm 102’s affliction, it stands as a declaration of what the God of the exile is really like. It will appear again later in the plan. Today read it as the answer to what Jeremiah and the psalmists have been asking: what is God like when we have failed?
observation: “Bless the LORD, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy name!” (v. 1).
“Who forgives all your iniquity, who heals all your diseases” (v. 3).
“The LORD works righteousness and justice for all who are oppressed” (v. 6).
“The LORD is merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love” (v. 8).
“He does not deal with us according to our sins, nor repay us according to our iniquities” (v. 10).
“As far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions from us” (v. 12).
“As a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him. For he knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust” (vv. 13-14).
interpretation:
David begins by speaking to his own soul. He commands himself to bless the LORD, and to remember. “Forget not all his benefits.” The psalm’s work is remembering, since we are forgetful. Then he lists them: forgiveness, healing, redemption from the pit, a crown of steadfast love, and satisfaction with good, so that your youth is renewed like the eagle’s. Forgiveness is the first item, and it is the benefit that makes the rest possible.

In verses 6 to 8, David recalls the way God made himself known to Moses: merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love. This is the self-description from Exodus 34:6, which Jonah quoted, and which echoes through the Bible. And the psalm unpacks it. God does not keep his anger forever. He does not deal with us according to our sins. The heavens are high above the earth, but his steadfast love is greater than that. The east is far from the west, and that is how far he has removed our transgressions.

Here is the point for the unit. This psalm is true even in exile. The exile was real judgment, and it was a sign that God deals with sin. But it was not the whole story. He did not repay them according to their iniquities. He kept a remnant. He promised to bring them back.

Verses 13 to 14 give the reason: God is like a father who knows his children. “He knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust.” God is not surprised by our weakness. He is gentle with it. The psalm ends by calling the angels, the mighty ones, and all creation to bless the LORD, and then returns to the beginning: “Bless the LORD, O my soul.”
connection: Ephesians 1:7 says that in Christ we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses. Hebrews 8:12 and 10:17 promise that God will remember our sins no more. Romans 8:15 says that we cry, “Abba! Father!” Luke 15:20 shows the father who ran to meet his son. 1 John 1:9 promises forgiveness and cleansing. Micah 7:18-19 says he casts all our sins into the depths of the sea.
application:
Write down five of God’s benefits to you, and thank him for each.

Preach to your own soul: say aloud “Bless the LORD, O my soul” when you feel low.

Rest in the truth that God remembers that you are dust. Bring your weakness to him without fear.
prayerPrompts: Bless the LORD with all that is within you.
Name a benefit of his that you do not want to forget.
Thank him for his love as high as the heavens.
